title: Confession and anointing
hookLine: Catholics and Orthodox confess to a priest; Anglicans may; most Protestants confess to God directly or to a friend (James 5:16)

cards: A secret can sit in the chest like a stone. Something done, something said, something hidden. Days go by, and it gets heavier, not lighter.
Then one evening it finally comes out, to a friend, a partner, a parent, in a shaky voice. It doesn't disappear. But often, it loosens.
A short letter in the New Testament, from James, puts this in one plain sentence, right next to another practice: oil and prayer for the sick.

teach.h: CALL THE ELDERS, ANOINT WITH OIL.
teach.b: From James chapter five, in the King James Bible: "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord."

teach.h: CONFESS YOUR FAULTS ONE TO ANOTHER.
teach.b: Then: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed." Oil for the sick, honest words for wrongs done. Start with confession.
Catholics and Orthodox Christians confess their sins to a priest in a sacrament; Catholics call it reconciliation or penance.
The priest speaks words of absolution, forgiveness in God's name, and he is bound never to reveal what he's heard.

teach.h: TO A PRIEST, TO GOD, TO A FRIEND.
teach.b: In many Orthodox churches, the person stands before an icon of Christ with the priest beside them, and the priest calls himself only a witness.
Anglicans offer private confession too, with an old saying: all may, none must, some should.
Most Protestants confess directly to God, and some also to a trusted friend or small group, taking James literally: one to another.
A line from John's first letter is often said: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins." Now anointing.
Catholics call it the anointing of the sick; it was once given mostly to the dying, and today it's for anyone seriously ill or facing surgery.

Orthodox Christians call it holy unction, and in many churches everyone is anointed during Holy Week. Some Protestant churches, Pentecostal ones among them, anoint the sick and pray, as James describes.
Words said out loud, oil on the skin: nobody should carry sickness or guilt alone.

how: Catholic and Orthodox Christians confess to a priest and receive absolution, and are anointed with oil when seriously ill; Anglicans may confess privately; most Protestants confess to God directly or to a trusted friend, and many churches anoint and pray for the sick.

games.q: someone in your church is seriously ill. according to James 5, what should they do?
o: keep it quiet and pray alone.
call for the elders to pray and anoint them with oil.

games.why: "let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil." illness isn't meant to be carried alone.

practice: Let one real thing you've been carrying come to mind: not the worst thing you've ever done, just something from this week, a sharp word, a small lie, a way you let someone down.
Don't argue or explain; just name it plainly to yourself.
If you pray, confess it to God in your own words, quietly or out loud, and sit with the promise of forgiveness; if you don't, say it to the silence and notice what happens to the weight.

wordCard.voice: Absolution, the priest's words of forgiveness spoken in God's name after confession, one of two practices James paired: honest words and healing oil.

carryVoice: Your line: said out loud, it loosens. The stone gets smaller in the air. That's day one hundred fifty-four.
